summary:
Fire seasons in Indonesia bring haze crises, and NASA has watched them from space for 25 years. But that record is split across three satellite sensors that count fires differently: VIIRS sees
about five times more hotspots than MODIS over the same land. Suomi NPP stopped on November 2, 2026, and MODIS is
retiring. So a raw count from 2005 cannot be compared with one from 2025.

Burn Calendar harmonizes 28.9 million NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS, VIIRS Suomi NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20 into one
consistent monthly record in NOAA-20 units, from November 2000 to now. The conversion is validated by holding out
each overlap year (error 10.9% for Indonesia, 7.6% for Northern Australia).

A free web app turns the record into answers. Is this month unusual? When is the fire season? Where is burning far
above normal? It has a pixel time machine and games for the public, an Analyst View with trend tests, a season
tracker, early signals and open CSV/JSON data for responders, and any province or a box you draw.
details:
Full project booklet (7 pages, PDF): https://alfanditora.github.io/burn-calendar/booklet.pdf

What it does.

Burn Calendar answers one question for anyone, from a disaster agency to a student: is this fire season worse than normal, and where? It turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections over Indonesia (and Northern Australia, to show the method travels) into one consistent monthly record.

How it works.

  1. Download: the NASA FIRMS area API for MODIS, VIIRS Suomi NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20. Standard (archive) data for the history, near-real-time data only where the archive ends.
  2. Clean: keep confident detections; remove volcanoes, gas flares and offshore sources using the FIRMS type flags.
  3. Count: inside real country and province borders, per month and per 25 km map square.
  4. Calibrate: chain the sensors on the years they overlap: MODIS × 5.10 → Suomi NPP × 1.01 → NOAA-20, with a drift check for the MODIS satellites' changing orbits.
  5. Validate: hold out each overlap year, predict it and report the error (10.9% Indonesia, 7.6% Northern Australia). An independent check against FIRMS's own Country Yearly Summary agrees within 2.2% (MODIS, 2001–2025) and 1.4% (NOAA-20, 2019–2025).
  6. Analyse: Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen's slope, the anomaly against the median of the same month in earlier years, the fire-season months, and an early-signal hindcast.

What people see.

  • Explore & Play (public): a pixel time machine of every month since 2000; a "Routine or unusual?" map, because a hotspot is not always a wildfire (farm, clearing, peat and planned burns look alike from space); four games with badges; and "What can I do?" advice for smoky days.
  • Analyst View (researchers, planners, emergency managers): the burning-activity calendar with CSV download, anomaly badge, trend test, season tracker, early signal, the most unusual places, a situation brief to copy or print, and open CSV/JSON files with the method and validation.
  • Any area: 4 featured areas, any of 33 Indonesian provinces and 3 Australian states, or a box you draw on the map. Every view has a shareable link and works on a phone.

What it found (Indonesia).

2015 was the worst year on record (812,705 hotspots, the Southeast Asian haze crisis). The long-term trend is falling (Mann-Kendall p = 0.018, about −11,151 hotspots per year). But October 2026 was +504% against a usual October, the most since 2015. In 12 of 15 years, a quiet June–July meant a quiet August–October peak: an early hint for planners, a historical pattern and not a forecast.

Benefits and intended impact.

One consistent record across the MODIS → VIIRS handover, just as Suomi NPP has stopped and MODIS is retiring. Plain answers for the public and numbers with their error for analysts. Free, no login, open data. Intended users: disaster agencies (such as BNPB and provincial BPBD), peatland and plantation managers, researchers and the public.

How it is creative.

It joins three sensors into one unit instead of showing them side by side; it answers "routine or unusual?" instead of calling every hotspot a wildfire; and it wraps a rigorous record in a pixel-art atlas and games, so the same numbers serve a responder and a student.

Factors we considered.

Honest limits are shown in the app: hotspots are not burned area, cloud and smoke hide some fires, the record is monthly (for live fires the app links to the NASA FIRMS Fire Map), and converted counts are estimates whose error is reported for each area. Small provinces show "too few fires" instead of noisy percentages. We never invent data, every threshold lives in one settings file, one command rebuilds everything, and 32 automated tests pass.

Next steps.

Early warnings for disaster agencies, the full analysis for every province, peat and land-cover maps to separate farm burning from forest and peat fires, NOAA-21 with monthly updates, and an AI plain-language brief with every number checked against the data.

Tools, languages, hardware.

Python (pandas, NumPy, pyarrow, shapely, pymannkendall, requests, pytest) for the data pipeline; HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework, canvas pixel art) for the app; GitHub Pages for hosting; a Windows laptop. Demo video: Playwright with Chrome, FFmpeg and edge-tts.
